title: Choose the data
summary: Separate a book title from its physical copies. Use stable IDs and links to keep the library facts clear without repeating every detail.
introduction: A library may own three copies of the same book. The title tells us what the book is, but each copy can sit on a different shelf. A good data plan keeps these two ideas separate.
learningObjectives: Choose the facts a library needs to store
Use stable IDs to connect records
Explain why a title is not enough to identify a copy

blocks.text: A **data model** describes the facts we store and how they connect. A record is a group of facts about one thing. A field is one named fact inside a record.
A book record describes a title and author. A copy record describes one physical copy. The copy has its own ID and a bookId that points to the matching book record.
An **ID** is a label used to identify a record. Keep it stable when a title or shelf changes. Two books can share a title, so the title alone is not a safe unique ID.
Keep a fact in one clear place when possible. Storing the same author name on every copy means fixing the same spelling in many places. A link lets several copies share one book description.

items: Create book 17 with title Moon and author Asha. Create book 18 with the same title but author Ben.
Create copies 203 and 204 with bookId 17. Their shelves are B2 and B3.
Create copy 205 with bookId 18. It belongs to the other book, even though the title matches.
Find copies by the stable book ID, then show their copy IDs and shelves.

blocks.title: Choose the data example
Expected result
blocks.content:
Moon by Asha
copies: 2
203 on B2, 204 on B3

blocks.text: This is a tiny model stored in browser memory. It helps us see the links; it is not a database. A database design can add rules that reject duplicate IDs and links to missing records.
Borrowing adds another kind of record: a loan. A loan can link a copy to a learner and its due date. Keep only the learner information the task really needs, and use fictional values for practice.
A lookup may find no book. A real service must handle that case before reading book.title. This example deliberately uses a book ID that is present.

Decide what a delete means. If a book still has copies or loan history, deleting its record may leave broken links. You could reject the delete or mark the book as retired, depending on the library's rules.
Repeating a fact can make some reads easier, but then updates need a rule to keep the copies correct. That choice should be deliberate, not an accident.

items: Add copy 206 with bookId 17 and shelf D1. Predict the result.
The book still prints Moon by Asha. The copy count becomes 3, and the last line also includes 206 on D1. Book 18 stays separate.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not use a title or shelf as the only ID. Titles can match other titles, and a copy can move to another shelf.
